sceneHappening: Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon and asks him to receive him as a beloved brother
summary: Paul, "a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother," write to Philemon, "our beloved fellow worker, to the beloved Apphia, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the assembly in your house," with grace and peace. Paul thanks his God always, "making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and of the faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all the saints," and prays "that the fellowship of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus. For we have much joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother." "Therefore though I have all boldness in Christ to command you that which is appropriate, yet for love's sake I rather beg, being such a one as Paul, the aged, but also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. I beg you for my child, whom I have become the father of in my chains, Onesimus, who once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me. I am sending him back. Therefore receive him, that is, my own heart, whom I desired to keep with me, that on your behalf he might serve me in my chains for the Good News. But I was willing to do nothing without your consent, that your goodness would not be as of necessity, but of free will. For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while, that you would have him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord." "If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it (not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self besides). Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in the Lord. Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say." Paul asks Philemon to "prepare a guest room for me, for I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you." Epaphras, "my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus," greets him, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, "my fellow workers." "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen."
whySettingMatters: Slavery was a normal part of the Roman world, and slaves made up a large share of the population of cities. A slave who left his owner without permission was a runaway, and the law could punish him severely. The usual reading of this letter is that Onesimus ran away (perhaps after wronging Philemon, as the talk of a debt suggests), met Paul in prison, and became a believer; Paul now sends him back. Another reading is that Onesimus did not simply run but went to Paul as a friend of the household, hoping that Paul would intercede, which Roman law allowed. The letter does not say, and Paul writes carefully: he mentions Onesimus by name only in 1:10, after the thanks and the appeal to love. Onesimus's name means "useful," and Paul plays on it in 1:11, "once useless... now useful." Paul does not say outright that Philemon must free Onesimus; he says "more than a slave, a beloved brother" (1:16), asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul, and says he is confident that Philemon "will do even beyond what I say" (1:21). Whether that means freedom, or sending him back to serve Paul, or something else has been debated for centuries, and the letter leaves the matter with Philemon. It is also true that the letter does not call slavery wrong, and some have used it to defend slavery; most readers have seen in it the beginning of the thought that, in Christ, the master and the slave are equal, a thought Paul states in Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11. Paul takes on a legal and financial responsibility (1:18-19): a letter signed in his own hand worked like a promissory note. The letter is sent with Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9), where Onesimus is called "the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you."

questions: Paul says he could command but prefers to appeal "for love's sake." What does it say about his understanding of authority that he chooses persuasion?
"No longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother." What do you think Paul is asking Philemon to do, and how do you know?
Paul offers to pay any debt "with my own hand." What does it mean to stand surety for someone else, and what did it cost Paul?
The letter was read aloud to the whole church in Philemon's house. How would that change the way Philemon answered?
